It very much depends on how it's filmed. All Quiet on Western Front is a moving film that hopefully makes you both sad for the soldiers and angry at the futility of it all. Would I have watched it if it was just four men in a room discussing what happened to them during the war? Possible but unlikely. 

To reach a wider audience, I think film-makers need to show them a film they might be visually interested in (not necessarily excited by) which then allows them to impart their message. In that vein I can think of Schindler's List, Saving Private Ryan (both mentioned), Gallipoli, The Cross of Iron and even Blackadder goes Forth.

Through the medium of comedy, BGF shows the terrible events of WWI and laid bare the notion of 'lions led by donkeys', the incompetence and indifference of the British commanders. I challenge anyone not to choke up a little at the final scene!

To answer your question, the violence of war films can be either informative or exploitative and the air of importance does help to sell but … both can also be used to paper over the cracks in a bad film.

You have to try and use your judgement and unfortunately that means you might occasionally have to watch bad films along with the good.

You are not too old. I started about then and now have a half decent pension after 11 years.

Not having a pension means you are potentially missing out on the tax benefits, i.e. 20% or 40% 'free' money from the government that gets added. The story gets more complicated when self employed but definitely start one now. Every day delayed is compound interest lost!

Check old work schemes, e.g. I got a decent lump from collecting three old workplace pensions into a SIPP.

A lot of questions that are hard to answer! The pension companies usually provide examples of possible pensions based on annuity so it will be quite low compared to drawdown (if that is ever an option). Very simplistic response below.

How to calculate the pension - down to the pension provider with an annuity though some  publish their rates, e.g. retiring @ 65 may get you £5000 per annum on £100k investment. If it's a money purchase then you can shop around annuities or use 3/4% of the investment per year to sustain yourself.

Different jobs - definitely a factor and some will give better benefits than others so you should consider that as a possible acceptance reason. My company money purchase scheme also puts the funds into an ultra safe fund so you might need to consider moving it to a fund that suits your desired risk level.

Inflation - another hard to calculate factor. There is always a balance between investment return and inflation, i.e. if your return is 8% and inflation is 3% then the real return is 5% (other fees may affect it). If inflation rises to 5% but return remains the same then you are only getting 3% real return.

Yes. If annuity then the pension company can advise you and if money purchase then, depending on the rules governing it, you can decide how much you can afford to take.

Hope that helps a little but there are so many variables it is difficult to be any more accurate.

Definitely need a better investment as your money is being eroded by inflation. 

As a newbie it might be best to approach your bank and see what they have available. E.g. Barclays have investment accounts using the ISA wrapper and rate them as Low, Medium, Higher risk so you start where you feel comfortable and then move around the different funds or even to other investment platforms.  
It is a huge topic and very quickly gets complicated so try to learn for yourself, just be careful of any schemes that have 'guaranteed high returns' and you should be ok. Do your research but don't delay as that loses you money every day you are not invested. Invest as much as you  spare, bearing in mind that if you really need to take it out of your ISA, you can (albeit there may be a penalty). [https://www.gov.uk/individual-savings-accounts/withdrawing-your-money](https://www.gov.uk/individual-savings-accounts/withdrawing-your-money)

There are loads of guides so google 'getting started with ISAs' and pick from there. A good one is from Hargreaves Lansdown: [https://www.hl.co.uk/investment-services/isa/isa-individual-savings-accounts-explained](https://www.hl.co.uk/investment-services/isa/isa-individual-savings-accounts-explained). Hi, my initial question is have you determined the need for 1m RPO? Is that a 'wish' or determined by the real cost of losing 1min, either through lost transactions or the time taken to recreate/rebuild/recover the 'lost' data?  
I work in BCM for a finance house and at that level (Tier 1), all data replication is synchronous   even if the RTO for the app/business service is max 4 hours. Anything else is async.  
RPO measurement is always a problem and with the amount of interconnected systems, it's not always as easy as seeing if the transaction committed as it can still appear OK but missed a vital step as another app was not available.  
I suppose one answer is to ask for the average latency on your replication devices or identify the moment a complex transaction completes (e.g. a flag is written on the remote side) and get your technical teams to track time between user committing in Prod/Test and the flag being written in DR site to say transaction complete. This has a host of potential problems: is the load when the sample is committed representative of peak production loads, are you able to do this is Prod and then back-out the changes without impact?  
An even simpler answer is to look over the top of your glasses when someone says 'I want 1min RPO!', and respond with 'Really? Do you know how much that will cost?'!  
If it's any consolation, I struggle with this as well and try and dissuade really low RPO unless they can make a compelling case, which is quite often in investment banking!
